question: Phase-to-phase stator resistance is an ATS electrical test on AC induction machines rated:
choices: Only when the PI is already below 1.0
explanation: 7.15.1.B.4 calls for the phase-to-phase stator resistance test at 2300 V and above. It sits beside the insulation-resistance test, not instead of the polarization index.

question: Motor branch-circuit wires are sized from:
choices: The Code table full-load current, at 125%
explanation: NEC 430.6(A) sends wire, disconnect, and the branch short-circuit device to the table current. 430.22 is 125% of that table value. The nameplate is what the separate overload uses. Sizing copper from the nameplate is how the wire comes out light.

question: The separate overload on a motor branch is set from:
explanation: NEC 430.6(A)(2) and 430.32 use the nameplate for the overload. The table current is for wire, disconnect, and the branch short-circuit device. Mixing those two currents is the classic miss.

question: On a motor branch, the overload and the breaker do different jobs. Which statement matches Article 430?
choices: The overload clears short circuits; the breaker only protects against a stall
The overload protects against overload and failure to start; the breaker or fuse is the short-circuit and ground-fault device
They are sized from the same nameplate current and the same table
The feeder breaker is allowed the same next-size-up as the branch
explanation: Part III is the overload, from nameplate current. Part IV is the branch short-circuit device, from table current and Table 430.52. A feeder under 430.62 does not get the branch’s next-size-up. Swapping those roles leaves a stalled motor on a breaker that may never see the overload.

question: ATS 7.15.1.B.2 splits the insulation-resistance test on an AC induction machine by size:
choices: Every machine gets a one-minute spot test only
Above 200 horsepower, ten minutes and a polarization index; 200 horsepower and less, one minute and a 60/30 dielectric-absorption ratio
Above 200 horsepower, a DC hipot instead of insulation resistance
explanation: ATS 7.15.1.B.2 assigns the ten-minute polarization index to machines over 200 horsepower and the one-minute 60/30 ratio to smaller machines. IEEE 43-2013 clause 5.4 defines that index as the 10-minute resistance divided by the 1-minute resistance. The ATS floors are PI not less than 2.0 and DAR not less than 1.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.15.1.B.2 and D.2; ref. IEEE 43-2013, clause 5.4

question: ATS 7.15.1.B.8 calls for an insulation-resistance test on:
choices: Insulated bearings, to the manufacturer’s data
explanation: An insulated bearing that is shorted circulates shaft current. The test follows the manufacturer’s published data, and D.8 compares the result with that data or with similar machines.

question: ATS 7.15.1.B.12 on an AC machine is a check that:
choices: The oil neutralization number is zero
explanation: Space heaters keep the winding dry while the machine is shut down. The insulation-resistance test does not prove the heater. Verify the heater itself.

question: ATS 7.15.1.A.10 says resistance-temperature-detector circuits on a machine must:
choices: Be disconnected for the polarization-index test and left that way
Read zero ohms to the frame
explanation: The RTD wiring is checked against the drawings. A later electrical test measures the RTD circuit resistance. Neither step is a 10 kV insulation test of the detector.

question: ATS 7.15.1.B.10 tests the motor starter:
choices: As part of the polarization index
Only if the machine is under 200 horsepower
explanation: The machine section does not restate the starter procedure. It points at 7.16. The insulation-resistance test of the winding is a different line.

question: An optional surge-comparison test passes ATS 7.15.1.D.7 when, by the end of the test:
choices: There is no distress, no insulation failure, and the waveforms nest
One phase rings at a different frequency and that is ignored
The polarization index is the only recorded number
explanation: The surge test looks for a winding that will not match its neighbors. Nesting waveforms and no failure are the pass. It is optional, and it does not replace insulation resistance.

question: In ATS 7.15.1, vibration under load and current-signature analysis are:
choices: Required before the one-minute insulation-resistance test
explanation: Both are marked optional, and both require the machine to be running under load. The insulation-resistance test is the required electrical test and does not wait on them.

question: Partial discharge on an AC induction machine in ATS 7.15.1.B.16 is:
choices: The required pass/fail in place of polarization index
Required on every machine under 200 horsepower
explanation: The machine PD test is marked optional. The required insulation test is still the IEEE 43 insulation-resistance test, with a PI or a DAR depending on horsepower.

question: You're planning PI tests on a plant's rotating machines. Where is a polarization index not applicable?
choices: Squirrel-cage rotor bars that are not insulated from the rotor body, and field windings with bare copper
A winding whose 1-minute resistance is 100 megohms
explanation: Those conductors do not show an absorption current, so the 10-minute ratio does not describe insulation. A wound rotor or a taped salient-pole winding can still be indexed. ATS 7.15.1 applies the PI to the insulated stator test, not to a squirrel-cage rotor.

question: Which ATS test is written for synchronous machines and is not in the induction-motor list?
choices: Insulation resistance of the rotating field and exciter windings
A 60/30 ratio on a 50 hp induction motor
explanation: 7.15.2.B.14 is insulation resistance of the main rotating field, the exciter field, and the exciter armature, in accordance with IEEE 43. Field resistance and the field-discharge resistor are in the same section. An induction machine has no rotating field winding to test.

question: Compared with an across-the-line start, a usual advantage of an adjustable-speed drive is:
choices: A 10-minute polarization index of 1.0 used as a drive pass/fail
A vacuum-pressure limit on the stator
explanation: A drive brings voltage and frequency up together, so the motor does not have to draw across-the-line locked-rotor current. That lower starting inrush is the usual reason to use a drive. ATS-2025 tests motor starters in 7.16 and adjustable-speed drives in 7.17. Section 7.17 does not print a numeric inrush comparison against an across-the-line start. The comparison is engineering fundamentals. Test the starter to 7.16 and the drive to 7.17.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (drive starting current); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.17 and 7.16

question: Jogging a motor on first start is recalled as a rotation check. In the texts read for this bank:
choices: ATS 7.15.1 prints the word jog and a required bump test
That sentence was not found; phase rotation is explicitly required on the engine-generator section
explanation: Section 7.15.1 has no jog or bump-test line. Section 7.22.1.B.3 requires phase rotation and phasing on a generator. ATS 4.1 item 6 leaves the owner to decide who runs the low-voltage motor rotation test, so motor rotation is mentioned in the ATS, though not as a required bump test in 7.15.1. Do not grade a recalled jog as a line of 7.15.1.

question: On a medium-voltage motor starter, ATS 7.16.1.2 says the overload rating is:
choices: Checked against the application and set from the coordination study when it is adjustable
The same as the cable VLF voltage
explanation: Adjustable or programmable protection is set to the study. If the manufacturer publishes no protection settings, the test values point at section 7.9. The contactor itself still gets an insulation-resistance test.

question: With no manufacturer voltage, insulation resistance of a medium-voltage starter contactor is:
choices: Table 100.1, one minute, phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground with the contactor closed, and across each open contact
Optional, because the MAC test replaces it
explanation: 7.16.1.2.B.1 is that insulation-resistance test. The magnetron test on a vacuum interrupter is optional and does not replace it. Control wiring, when tested, is 500 V or 1000 V dc depending on the cable rating.

question: In an IEEE 95-2002 step (stepped-voltage) dc test on a stator winding, the first voltage step is usually held about how long, and why?
choices: 1 minute, to get a spot reading
About 10 minutes, to get absorption ratio, insulation resistance, and polarization index
explanation: In a step test the dc voltage rises in uniform or graded steps. The first step is usually held about 10 minutes so you can determine absorption ratio, insulation resistance, and polarization index. Later steps can be timed to linearize the absorption current. Source: IEEE 95-2002, 3.23.

question: A small motor on resilient mounts, NEMA frame 210 or under, is checked uncoupled at no load. Under ATS acceptance limits, unfiltered housing vibration velocity for grade A should not exceed:
explanation: Table 100.10 lists grade A, resilient mounting, frame 210 and under, at 2.4 mils pk-pk or 0.15 in/s pk. Grade B is tighter (0.06 in/s pk for that frame). The table is derived from NEMA MG 1 Section 7.8 and applies to machines uncoupled at no load. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.10.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.10 and notes 1-2 (from NEMA MG 1-2021, 7.8, Table 7-11)

question: Per NEMA MG 1-2016 (Rev 2018) Part 12, what's the one-minute high-potential test voltage for the stator of a new 460 V, 50 hp induction motor?
explanation: For induction motors over 1/2 hp the stator test voltage is 1000 V plus twice rated voltage, but not less than 1500 V: 1000 + 2 × 460 = 1920 V. MG 1 also warns that repeated hipot applications are not recommended because they overstress the insulation. Source: NEMA MG 1-2016 (Rev 2018) Part 12, 12.3.

question: A general-purpose 460 V motor is fed from a VFD. Per NEMA MG 1-2016 (Rev 2018) Part 30, what terminal voltage stress can it see without significant life reduction?
choices: Vpeak ≤ 1 kV with rise time ≥ 2 µs
Vpeak ≤ 3.1 × rated with rise time ≥ 0.1 µs
Vpeak ≤ 2.04 × rated with rise time ≥ 1 µs
Any peak, as long as rms is 460 V
explanation: For general-purpose motors rated 600 V or less, Part 30 assumes no significant service-life loss if Vpeak at the motor terminals stays at or below 1 kV with rise time at least 2 µs. Above 600 V the limit is 2.04 × rated with rise time at least 1 µs. The 3.1 × rated value belongs to Part 31 definite-purpose inverter-fed motors. Source: NEMA MG 1-2016 (Rev 2018) Part 30, 30.2.2.8.

question: A definite-purpose inverter-fed motor rated 460 V is used on a drive whose input doesn't exceed motor rating. Per NEMA MG 1-2016 (Rev 2018) Part 31, its insulation must withstand a terminal peak of about:
explanation: Part 31 motors rated 600 V or less are designed to withstand Vpeak ≤ 1.1 × 2 × √2 × Vrated ≈ 3.1 × Vrated with rise time ≥ 0.1 µs: 3.1 × 460 ≈ 1426 V. If drive input voltage exceeds motor rating, the peak needs to be worked out more carefully. Source: NEMA MG 1-2016 (Rev 2018) Part 31, 31.4.4.2.

question: The NEMA MG 1-2016 (Rev 2018) Part 30 harmonic derating curve (Figure 30-1) is meant for which case?
choices: A VFD-fed motor running below base speed
A constant-speed motor at rated frequency on a bus whose voltage has harmonic content
explanation: Clause 30.1.2 has you multiply rated horsepower by the Figure 30-1 factor when a motor at rated conditions sees voltage with non-fundamental components. It assumes only odd, non-triplen harmonics and negligible unbalance, and it does not apply to operation at other than rated frequency or from adjustable-voltage or adjustable-frequency supplies. Source: NEMA MG 1-2016 (Rev 2018) Part 30, 30.1.2.
